'''''Adiantum pedatum''''', the '''northern maidenhair fern''', is a [[species]] of [[fern]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Pteridaceae]],<ref name="Christenhusz-2011"/> [[native plant|native]] to moist [[forest]]s in eastern [[North America]]. Like other ferns in the genus, the name maidenhair refers to the slender, shining black [[Stipe (botany)|stipes]]. Taxonomy classification disputes occur due to the distribution of ''A. Pedatum'' in both North America and East Asia.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Irfan |first1=Muhammad |last2=Jan |first2=Gul |last3=Jan |first3=Farzana Gul |last4=Murad |first4=Waheed |date=2021 |title=Taxonomy and spore morphology of genus Adiantum (Vittarioideae; Pteridaceae) from Pakistan |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/jemt.23835 |journal=Microscopy Research and Technique |language=en |volume=84 |issue=11 |pages=2727–2736 |doi=10.1002/jemt.23835 |pmid=34051004 |issn=1097-0029}}</ref>

==Description==
''A. pedatum'' grows {{convert|30|-|75|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall, and is [[deciduous]]. ''A. pedatum'' has clusters of [[Spore|spores]] on the underside of the [[leaf margin]]s of the curved [[Lobes (leaf)|lobes]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Paris |first1=Cathy A. |last2=Windham |first2=Michael D. |date=1988 |title=A Biosystematic Investigation of the Adiantum pedatum Complex in Eastern North America |journal=Systematic Botany |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=240–255 |doi=10.2307/2419103 |jstor=2419103 |bibcode=1988SysBo..13..240P |issn=0363-6445}}</ref> The key features of the northern maidenhair fern include fine, frilly [[Frond|fronds]] divided into curved stalks, reddish-brown stems, and crosiers that emerge pink in the spring.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Adiantum pedatum (Common Maidenhair, Northern Maidenhair, Northern Maidenhair Fern) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/adiantum-pedatum/ |access-date=2025-12-07 |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref> ''A. pedatum'' is the most northern species within the genus, found in higher latitudes and best grown in drained soil in shaded areas.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Paris |first1=Cathy A. |last2=Windham |first2=Michael D. |date=1988 |title=A Biosystematic Investigation of the Adiantum pedatum Complex in Eastern North America |journal=Systematic Botany |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=240–255 |doi=10.2307/2419103 |jstor=2419103 |bibcode=1988SysBo..13..240P |issn=0363-6445}}</ref> The greatest issues with [[Taxonomic classification|classifying]] the species occur within the ''A. pedatum'' group due to the variation of [[species]] recognition and large [[genetic diversity]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Paris |first1=Cathy A. |last2=Windham |first2=Michael D. |date=1988 |title=A Biosystematic Investigation of the Adiantum pedatum Complex in Eastern North America |journal=Systematic Botany |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=240–255 |doi=10.2307/2419103 |jstor=2419103 |bibcode=1988SysBo..13..240P |issn=0363-6445}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Adiantum pedatum'' was [[species description|described]] by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] in ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' in 1753 (the official starting point of modern botanical nomenclature). He referred to earlier descriptions, all based on material from eastern North America.{{sfn|Linnaeus|1753|p=1095}} Linnaeus' own herbarium contains one specimen, collected by [[Pehr Kalm]].

Specimens collected in [[Unalaska, Alaska|Unalaska]] and [[Kodiak Island]] by Chamisso and Langsdorf were referred to as ''Adiantum boreale'' by Presl in 1836, although he did not provide a species description to accompany the name. Ruprecht, in 1845, called the Alaskan material ''A. pedatum'' var. ''aleuticum'', and created var. ''kamtschaticum'' for material collected in [[Kamchatka Peninsula|Kamchatka]] by Carl Merck and Pallas. In 1857, E. J. Lowe noted that Wallich and Cantor had collected the species in northern India, and that material from the western United States ranged as far south as California. <!-- Douglas & Barclay, fide Hook. --> It was one of the many species cited by [[Asa Gray]] as disjunct between Japan and both the eastern and western United States. By 1874, Hooker & Baker reported it as present in both Japan and Manchuria.

''A. pedatum'' is part of a group of similar species. The greatest issues with classifying the species occur within the group due to the variation of species recognition and large genetic diversity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Paris |first1=Cathy A. |last2=Windham |first2=Michael D. |date=1988 |title=A Biosystematic Investigation of the Adiantum pedatum Complex in Eastern North America |journal=Systematic Botany |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=240–255 |doi=10.2307/2419103 |jstor=2419103 |bibcode=1988SysBo..13..240P |issn=0363-6445}}</ref> Species that have been placed in the ''A. pedatum'' group include ''[[Adiantum aleuticum|A. aleuticum]]'' and ''[[Adiantum viridimontanum|A. viridimontanum.]]'' ''A. pedatum'' also resembles species such as ''A. myriosorum''.<ref name="Lu-2011">{{Cite journal |last1=Lu |first1=Jin-Mei |last2=Li |first2=De-Zhu |last3=Lutz |first3=Sue |last4=Soejima |first4=Akiko |last5=Yi |first5=Tingshuang |last6=Wen |first6=Jun |date=2011 |title=Biogeographic disjunction between eastern Asia and North America in the Adiantum pedatum complex (Pteridaceae) |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.3732/ajb.1100125 |journal=American Journal of Botany |language=en |volume=98 |issue=10 |pages=1680–1693 |doi=10.3732/ajb.1100125 |issn=1537-2197 |pmid=21965133|bibcode=2011AmJB...98.1680L |url-access=subscription }}</ref> These all have [[frond]]s distinctively bifurcated and with [[leaflet (botany)|pinnae]] on only one side.{{citation needed|date=November 2025}}

Some subspecies have been recognized,<ref name="Paris-1988">{{Cite journal |last1=Paris |first1=Cathy A. |last2=Windham |first2=Michael D. |date=1988 |title=A Biosystematic Investigation of the Adiantum pedatum Complex in Eastern North America |journal=Systematic Botany |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=240–255 |bibcode=1988SysBo..13..240P |doi=10.2307/2419103 |issn=0363-6445 |jstor=2419103}}</ref> but none are accepted by Plants of the World Online.<ref name=POWO_30004419-2/>

== Distribution and habitat ==
''A. pedatum'' is the most northern species within the genus, occupying regions in Eastern Asia (EA) and North America (NA), and categorized by a [[disjunct distribution]] due to climate and geological occurrence.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lu |first1=Jin-Mei |last2=Li |first2=De-Zhu |last3=Lutz |first3=Sue |last4=Soejima |first4=Akiko |last5=Yi |first5=Tingshuang |last6=Wen |first6=Jun |date=2011 |title=Biogeographic disjunction between eastern Asia and North America in the Adiantum pedatum complex (Pteridaceae) |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.3732/ajb.1100125 |journal=American Journal of Botany |language=en |volume=98 |issue=10 |pages=1680–1693 |doi=10.3732/ajb.1100125 |pmid=21965133 |bibcode=2011AmJB...98.1680L |issn=1537-2197|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The EA-NA disjunction of A. pedatum is a focal point for botanists and is speculated to have occurred due to multiple geographic events.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lu |first1=Jin-Mei |last2=Li |first2=De-Zhu |last3=Lutz |first3=Sue |last4=Soejima |first4=Akiko |last5=Yi |first5=Tingshuang |last6=Wen |first6=Jun |date=2011 |title=Biogeographic disjunction between eastern Asia and North America in the Adiantum pedatum complex (Pteridaceae) |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.3732/ajb.1100125 |journal=American Journal of Botany |language=en |volume=98 |issue=10 |pages=1680–1693 |doi=10.3732/ajb.1100125 |pmid=21965133 |bibcode=2011AmJB...98.1680L |issn=1537-2197|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Northern maidenhair fern grows best in shaded areas with [[Soil|humus-rich soil]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lu |first1=Jin-Mei |last2=Li |first2=De-Zhu |last3=Lutz |first3=Sue |last4=Soejima |first4=Akiko |last5=Yi |first5=Tingshuang |last6=Wen |first6=Jun |date=2011 |title=Biogeographic disjunction between eastern Asia and North America in the Adiantum pedatum complex (Pteridaceae) |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.3732/ajb.1100125 |journal=American Journal of Botany |language=en |volume=98 |issue=10 |pages=1680–1693 |doi=10.3732/ajb.1100125 |pmid=21965133 |bibcode=2011AmJB...98.1680L |issn=1537-2197|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Its preferred habitats are [[deciduous]] forests and at the base of rocky [[Mountain|mountains]] when adequate moisture is present.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lu |first1=Jin-Mei |last2=Li |first2=De-Zhu |last3=Lutz |first3=Sue |last4=Soejima |first4=Akiko |last5=Yi |first5=Tingshuang |last6=Wen |first6=Jun |date=2011 |title=Biogeographic disjunction between eastern Asia and North America in the Adiantum pedatum complex (Pteridaceae) |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.3732/ajb.1100125 |journal=American Journal of Botany |language=en |volume=98 |issue=10 |pages=1680–1693 |doi=10.3732/ajb.1100125 |pmid=21965133 |bibcode=2011AmJB...98.1680L |issn=1537-2197|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Fern distribution occurs through [[spore dispersal]] via wind, and does not rely on [[biotic factors]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Irfan |first1=Muhammad |last2=Jan |first2=Gul |last3=Jan |first3=Farzana Gul |last4=Murad |first4=Waheed |date=2021 |title=Taxonomy and spore morphology of genus Adiantum (Vittarioideae; Pteridaceae) from Pakistan |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/jemt.23835 |journal=Microscopy Research and Technique |language=en |volume=84 |issue=11 |pages=2727–2736 |doi=10.1002/jemt.23835 |pmid=34051004 |issn=1097-0029}}</ref> so ''A. pedatum'' is more susceptible to [[abiotic factors]] such as changes in environmental conditions.
[[File:Adiantum pedatum BW-1983-0000-0771.jpg|thumb|''A. pedatum'' from herbarium.]]

|first4=Narumi |last5=Soejima |first5=Akiko |last6=Li |first6=De-Zhu |last7=Wen |first7=Jun |last8=Lu |first8=Jin-Mei |date=2021-11-11 |title=Adiantum japonicum, a new species of the Adiantum pedatum == Life history ==
[[File:Adiantum pedatum JJK’1.jpg|thumb|Northern maidenhair fern.]]
''A. pedatum'' is a spore-producing, woody [[Flowering plant|flowering]] plant. The reproductive stages of ferns include the [[spore]], [[gametophyte]], [[sporeling]], and [[sporophyte]] stages.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Peck |first1=James H. |last2=Peck |first2=Carol J. |last3=Farrar |first3=Donald R. |date=1990 |title=Influences of Life History Attributes on Formation of Local and Distant Fern Populations |journal=American Fern Journal |volume=80 |issue=4 |pages=126–142 |doi=10.2307/1547200 |jstor=1547200 |bibcode=1990AmFJ...80..126P |issn=0002-8444}}</ref> Compared to other species of [[Fern|ferns]], ''A. pedatum''contains a high amount of fertile plants and produces a significant amount of spores for [[Seed dispersal|dispersal]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Peck |first1=James H. |last2=Peck |first2=Carol J. |last3=Farrar |first3=Donald R. |date=1990 |title=Influences of Life History Attributes on Formation of Local and Distant Fern Populations |journal=American Fern Journal |volume=80 |issue=4 |pages=126–142 |doi=10.2307/1547200 |jstor=1547200 |bibcode=1990AmFJ...80..126P |issn=0002-8444}}</ref> [[Long-distance dispersal]] is inferred to have occurred in the past.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Peck |first1=James H. |last2=Peck |first2=Carol J. |last3=Farrar |first3=Donald R. |date=1990 |title=Influences of Life History Attributes on Formation of Local and Distant Fern Populations |journal=American Fern Journal |volume=80 |issue=4 |pages=126–142 |doi=10.2307/1547200 |jstor=1547200 |bibcode=1990AmFJ...80..126P |issn=0002-8444}}</ref> 

Limitations in ''A. pedatum'' include [[spore]] production, retention and release.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Peck |first1=James H. |last2=Peck |first2=Carol J. |last3=Farrar |first3=Donald R. |date=1990 |title=Influences of Life History Attributes on Formation of Local and Distant Fern Populations |journal=American Fern Journal |volume=80 |issue=4 |pages=126–142 |doi=10.2307/1547200 |jstor=1547200 |bibcode=1990AmFJ...80..126P |issn=0002-8444}}</ref> There are continuing [[Life history trait|life history traits]] that affect [[reproduction]] including [[gametophyte]] establishment, persistence, [[Plant reproductive morphology|sexual status]], selecting for [[self-fertilization]] or [[outcrossing]], and new [[sporophyte]] establishment.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Peck |first1=James H. |last2=Peck |first2=Carol J. |last3=Farrar |first3=Donald R. |date=1990 |title=Influences of Life History Attributes on Formation of Local and Distant Fern Populations |journal=American Fern Journal |volume=80 |issue=4 |pages=126–142 |doi=10.2307/1547200 |jstor=1547200 |bibcode=1990AmFJ...80..126P |issn=0002-8444}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Irfan |first1=Muhammad |last2=Jan |first2=Gul |last3=Jan |first3=Farzana Gul |last4=Murad |first4=Waheed |date=2021 |title=Taxonomy and spore morphology of genus Adiantum (Vittarioideae; Pteridaceae) from Pakistan |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/jemt.23835 |journal=Microscopy Research and Technique |language=en |volume=84 |issue=11 |pages=2727–2736 |doi=10.1002/jemt.23835 |pmid=34051004 |issn=1097-0029}}</ref>
[[File:Adiantum pedatum.png|thumb|Artistic rendering of northern maidenhair fern.]]
Evolutionary changes including the [[Gene duplication|duplication]] of [[gene loci]], the occurrence of [[multivalence]] in [[Meiosis|meiotic sporocytes]], and a limited [[Geographic distribution of plants|geographic distribution]] all contribute toward the recent origin of the [[tetraploid]] in ''A. pedatum''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lu |first1=Jin-Mei |last2=Li |first2=De-Zhu |last3=Lutz |first3=Sue |last4=Soejima |first4=Akiko |last5=Yi |first5=Tingshuang |last6=Wen |first6=Jun |date=2011 |title=Biogeographic disjunction between eastern Asia and North America in the Adiantum pedatum complex (Pteridaceae) |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.3732/ajb.1100125 |journal=American Journal of Botany |language=en |volume=98 |issue=10 |pages=1680–1693 |doi=10.3732/ajb.1100125 |pmid=21965133 |bibcode=2011AmJB...98.1680L |issn=1537-2197}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barrington |first1=David S. |last2=Patel |first2=Nikisha R. |last3=Southgate |first3=Morgan W. |date=April 2020 |title=Inferring the impacts of evolutionary history and ecological constraints on spore size and shape in the ferns |journal=Applications in Plant Sciences |volume=8 |issue=4 |article-number=e11339 |doi=10.1002/aps3.11339 |doi-access=free |issn=2168-0450 |pmc=7186895 |pmid=32351800 |bibcode=2020AppPS...8E1339B }}</ref>

== Research focus ==
Research on ''A. pedatum'' focuses on the potential as [[anti-cancer]], [[Antioxidant|anti-oxidant]] and [[anti-inflammatory]] agents.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=January 2023 |title=The Antiproliferative Activity of Adiantum pedatum Extract and/or Piceatannol in Phenylhydrazine-Induced Colon Cancer in Male Albino Rats: The miR-145 Expression of the PI-3K/Akt/p53 and Oct4/Sox2/Nanog Pathways |url=https://www.mdpi.com/1420-3049/28/14/5543 |journal=Molecules |language=en |volume=28 |issue=14  |issn=1420-3049 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241204225252/https://www.mdpi.com/1420-3049/28/14/5543 |archive-date=4 December 2024}}</ref> There have been studies that found potential protective effects against colon cancer in ''A. pedatum''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tarek |first1=Khamis |last2=Diab, Abd Al-Aziz Abas |last3=H. |first3=Zahra, Mansour |last4=Ebrahim |first4=El-Dahmy, Samih |last5=Abd Al-Hameed, Basant Ahmed |last6=Adel |first6=Abdelkhalek |last7=A. |first7=Said, Mahmoud |last8=Hussein |first8=Abdellatif |last9=Mihaela |first9=Fericean, Liana |last10=Ioan |first10=Banatean-Dunea |last11=Hamed |first11=Arisha, Ahmed |last12=S. |first12=Attia, Mai |date=January 2023 |title=The Antiproliferative Activity of Adiantum pedatum Extract and/or Piceatannol in Phenylhydrazine-Induced Colon Cancer in Male Albino Rats: The miR-145 Expression of the PI-3K/Akt/p53 and Oct4/Sox2/Nanog Pathways |url=https://www.mdpi.com/1420-3049/28/14/5543 |journal=Molecules |language=en |volume=28 |issue=14 |doi=10.3390/molecule |doi-broken-date=11 August 2026 |doi-access=free |issn=1420-3049 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241204225252/https://www.mdpi.com/1420-3049/28/14/5543 |archive-date=2024-12-04}}</ref>
